name: ATMEGA328P-MU
title: ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 4 to 32 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash
summary: A family of low-power 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that run most of their 131 instructions in a single clock, reaching 20 MIPS at 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V and running down to 1.8 V at 4 MHz. The eight devices differ in memory, boot loader support and vector size: 4, 8, 16 or 32 Kbytes of Flash with 256 bytes to 1 Kbyte of EEPROM and 512 bytes to 2 Kbytes of SRAM. Each carries two 8-bit and one 16-bit timer with six PWM outputs, a real-time counter on its own 32 kHz oscillator, a 10-bit ADC with eight inputs (six on the SPDIP), a USART, SPI, a 2-wire (I2C) interface, an analog comparator, a watchdog on its own oscillator, a calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator and 23 I/O lines. ATMEGA328P-MU is the 32 Kbyte picoPower device in the 32-pad VQFN.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR, 32 x 8 working registers, 2-cycle hardware multiplier, up to 20 MIPS at 20 MHz
32 Kbytes Flash, 1 Kbyte EEPROM, 2 Kbytes SRAM
active 0.2 mA, power-down 0.1 µA, power-save 0.75 µA with 32 kHz RTC
10-bit, 8 channels in TQFP and VQFN, 6 in SPDIP
USART, SPI, 2-wire (I2C), two 8-bit and one 16-bit timer, six PWM, analog comparator, watchdog

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator between XTAL1 (PB6) and XTAL2 (PB7), each pin loaded by a capacitor to ground. C1 and C2 are always equal. For crystals of 0.9 MHz and up, 12 pF to 22 pF suits both the low power and the full swing oscillator; a ceramic resonator takes the values its own maker gives. The best value depends on the crystal, the stray capacitance and the electrical noise around it. The same hook-up serves TOSC1 and TOSC2 for a 32.768 kHz crystal, where each pin already carries an internal load of 18 pF (XTAL1/TOSC1) and 8 pF (XTAL2/TOSC2) and external capacitors are needed only for a crystal rated above 6 pF load.
notes: The full swing oscillator runs only from 2.7 V to 5.5 V.

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: An outside clock source drives XTAL1 (PB6) against the part's ground, with the CKSEL fuses at 0000; XTAL2 is left as the I/O pin PB7. The clock may run from 0 MHz to 20 MHz.
notes: The frequency may not move by more than 2% from one cycle to the next; for larger changes hold the part in reset, or change speed with the system clock prescaler.

circuits.title: ADC power connections
circuits.description: AVCC is fed from the digital VCC through a 10 µH series inductor, with 100 nF from AVCC to ground, so switching noise on VCC is filtered before it reaches the converter. The analog pins (ADC0 to ADC7, AREF, AVCC and the GND beside them) sit over a separate analog ground plane.
notes: The capacitor's ground and the GND pin next to AREF return to the analog ground plane.

circuits.title: debugWIRE connection
circuits.description: The target runs from a 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply on VCC with GND to ground, and the emulator's single dW line joins the RESET pin (PC6), which serves as the debug wire once DWEN is programmed.
notes: A pull-up on dW, if fitted, is 10 kΩ or larger; no capacitor or other reset source may be on the line.

circuits.title: Serial programming connection
circuits.description: An SPI programmer drives MOSI (PB3) and SCK (PB5), reads MISO (PB4) and holds RESET (PC6) low; VCC and AVCC take 1.8 V to 5.5 V, AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC. A clock goes to XTAL1 (PB6) only when the fuses select an external clock; on the internal oscillator XTAL1 is left free.

equations.note: Worked example at VCC = 2.0 V, F = 1 MHz: the idle current times one plus the percentage of each enabled module. The idle-current graph gives about 0.055 mA at this point; the product uses 0.045 mA.

operation.text: The eight devices share one design and differ only in memory size, boot loader support and interrupt vector size. The 168 and 328 devices use two-word vectors, the 48 and 88 one-word vectors. The 88, 168 and 328 devices have a separate boot loader section from which alone SPM may run, giving true read-while-write; the 48A/48PA have neither, and SPM runs from anywhere in Flash.
Qualification projects a retention failure rate well under 1 PPM: for 20 years at 85 °C, or 100 years at 25 °C.
Capacitive touch buttons, sliders and wheels are supported in software through the QTouch Library, with both QTouch and QMatrix acquisition.

A Harvard architecture with separate program and data buses and a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one executes, so one instruction completes per clock. The ALU takes two operands from the 32-register file and writes the result back in one cycle. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; every program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space. The 64 I/O locations sit at data addresses 0x20 - 0x5F; the extended I/O space at 0x60 - 0xFF is reachable only with ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between registers or between a register and a constant, and signed, unsigned and fractional multiplies on the on-chip multiplier. SREG is updated after every ALU operation, often making a separate compare unnecessary. SREG holds the global interrupt enable I, the bit store T, half carry H, sign S (N exclusive-or V), two's complement overflow V, negative N, zero Z and carry C. SREG is neither saved on entry to an interrupt nor restored on return; software must do it.

The 32 working registers map onto the first 32 data addresses (R0 at 0x00 to R31 at 0x1F) and most instructions reach all of them in one cycle. R26:R27, R28:R29 and R30:R31 pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing with fixed displacement, post-increment or pre-decrement; Z also points into Flash for table look-up.

The stack lives in SRAM and grows down from higher addresses; PUSH decrements SP. SP starts at the last SRAM address (RAMEND) and must point above 0x0100, the start of SRAM, and be set before any call or interrupt. SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH and SPL.
The CPU runs straight from the selected clock source with no internal division, giving up to 1 MIPS per MHz. A two-register ALU operation fetches, executes and writes back within one clock.

Each interrupt has its own vector and enable bit and runs only when the global I bit in SREG is set too. Vectors sit at the bottom of program memory by default; the lower the address, the higher the priority, RESET first and INT0 next. IVSEL in MCUCR moves the vectors to the start of the boot section and the BOOTRST fuse moves the reset vector there; programmed boot lock bits BLB02 or BLB12 can disable interrupts depending on where the program counter is. Taking an interrupt clears I; RETI sets it again, and software may set I to allow nesting. Flag-type interrupts are remembered while disabled and served by priority once enabled, and the hardware clears the flag on entry; writing a one also clears a flag. Level-type interrupts fire only while the condition lasts. After any return from an interrupt one more main-program instruction runs before a pending interrupt is served. CLI takes effect at once, so no interrupt runs after it, which protects timed sequences such as the EEPROM write. The instruction after SEI always runs before any pending interrupt, so SEI followed by SLEEP enters sleep first.

At least four clock cycles from the event to the vector, during which the program counter is pushed; the vector's jump takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four cycles on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. A return from interrupt takes four cycles, popping the two-byte program counter, adding two to SP and setting I.

4, 8, 16 or 32 Kbytes organised as 2K, 4K, 8K or 16K x 16, addressed by an 11, 12, 13 or 14-bit program counter, with at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. On the 88, 168 and 328 devices Flash splits into an application section and a boot loader section, each with its own lock bits, and the SPM instruction that writes the application section must sit in the boot section. Constant tables may sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The lowest data addresses hold the register file (32), the I/O registers (64), the extended I/O registers (160) and then 512, 1024, 1024 or 2048 bytes of SRAM, so 768, 1280, 1280 or 2303 locations in all. Five addressing modes reach all of it: direct (the whole space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from the base in Y or Z), plain indirect, and indirect with the pointer pre-decremented or post-incremented.
An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

256, 512, 512 or 1024 bytes in a separate data space, read and written a byte at a time, with at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. The access registers sit in I/O space. A read halts the CPU for four cycles and the data is ready at once; a write halts it for two cycles and then runs self-timed, 3.3 ms typical (26,368 cycles of the calibrated RC oscillator), so software can poll for completion.

A supply too low for the clock speed can corrupt the EEPROM in two ways: a write sequence needs a minimum voltage, and the CPU itself can misexecute. Holding the part in reset through low supply prevents both; the internal brown-out detector does it, or an external low-VCC reset circuit where the BOD levels do not fit. A write already running when reset arrives completes if the supply is still high enough.

Every I/O register and peripheral is in the I/O space. IN and OUT reach I/O addresses 0x00 - 0x3F; as data space with LD and ST, add 0x20. Registers at 0x00 - 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; these act only on the named bit, so they are safe on registers whose flags clear on writing one. The extended I/O registers (0x60 - 0xFF) need LDS/STS with SBRS, SBRC, SBR and CBR in place of IN, OUT, SBIS, SBIC, CBI and SBI. Reserved bits should be written zero, and reserved addresses never written. Three general purpose I/O registers (GPIOR0 at 0x1E, GPIOR1 at 0x2A, GPIOR2 at 0x2B) hold any data; GPIOR0 is bit-addressable.

To write: wait until EEPE is clear (and any SPM operation has finished, if a boot loader is present), load the address into EEAR and the data into EEDR, set EEMPE, then set EEPE within four cycles. Interrupts must be kept off across the EEMPE-EEPE sequence. To read: wait until EEPE is clear, load EEAR, set EERE and take the byte from EEDR. While a write is in progress EEAR cannot be changed and the EEPROM cannot be read.

clkCPU feeds the core, register file, status register and stack; clkI/O feeds most peripherals (timers, SPI, USART) and the external interrupt logic; clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, normally with clkCPU; clkASY clocks the asynchronous timer straight from a 32 kHz crystal or an outside clock so it can keep counting in sleep; clkADC is a separate domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can be stopped during a conversion to cut digital noise. TWI address recognition works in every sleep mode. Clocks to unused modules stop in the sleep modes.

The CKSEL3:0 Flash fuses pick the source: low power crystal, full swing crystal, low frequency crystal, internal 128 kHz RC, calibrated internal RC or external clock. The chosen clock goes to the AVR clock generator and on to the modules.

Parts ship running from the internal RC oscillator at 8.0 MHz with CKDIV8 programmed, so the system clock is 1.0 MHz, with the longest start-up time (CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10, CKDIV8 = 0). Every programming interface works with this setting.

After every other reset source releases, an internal reset is held for a time-out tTOUT counted on the watchdog oscillator, its length set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses (0, 4.1 ms or 65 ms typical at 5 V). It does not measure the supply, so it must outlast the VCC rise; otherwise use the brown-out detector, which holds reset until VCC is high enough and lets the time-out be disabled. Disabling the time-out without a brown-out detector is not recommended. A ripple counter then holds reset for a set number of oscillator cycles, from 6 for an outside clock up to 32K for a low frequency crystal. Waking from power-down or power-save counts only these start-up cycles, not the time-out.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. This oscillator swings XTAL2 less than rail to rail, draws the least power, cannot drive other clock inputs and is more prone to noise. CKSEL3:1 picks one of three frequency ranges from 0.4 MHz to 16 MHz; CKSEL0 with SUT1:0 picks the start-up time. C1 and C2 are equal.

The same amplifier with rail-to-rail swing on XTAL2, able to drive other clock inputs and better in noisy surroundings, at higher current than the low power oscillator. It covers 0.4 MHz to 20 MHz (CKSEL3:1 = 011) and works only with VCC from 2.7 V to 5.5 V.

Built for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal at very low power; the crystal's load capacitance and ESR both matter. Each pin carries an internal load (18 pF on XTAL1/TOSC1, 8 pF on XTAL2/TOSC2); a crystal rated above 6 pF load needs external capacitors. It is chosen with CKSEL 0100 or 0101, and SUT1:0 sets the extra delay from reset.

About 8.0 MHz with no external parts, dependent on voltage and temperature. At reset the hardware loads the factory calibration byte into OSCCAL; software may write OSCCAL for better accuracy than the factory setting gives. The watchdog oscillator still times the watchdog and the reset time-out when this clock is in use. CKSEL = 0010.
A low power 128 kHz clock, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C and not made for accuracy, chosen with CKSEL = 0011.

An outside clock of 0 MHz to 20 MHz drives XTAL1 with CKSEL = 0000. A cycle-to-cycle change of more than 2% can make the MCU misbehave; keep it in reset through larger changes, or use the system clock prescaler to change speed at run time.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock appears on CLKO (PB0), during reset too, taking over the pin's I/O function. Any source can be output; with the prescaler in use the divided clock comes out.

The timer oscillator uses the same crystal oscillator as the low frequency source, on TOSC1 and TOSC2, which share XTAL1 and XTAL2. The system clock must be at least four times the oscillator frequency, so the timer oscillator is usable only with the calibrated internal RC oscillator as the system clock. An outside clock may drive TOSC1 when EXTCLK in ASSR is set.

CLKPR divides the system clock (clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH) for any clock source, to save power when little processing is needed. Switching is glitch-free, and no intermediate frequency is higher than either the old or the new setting. To change CLKPS, write CLKPCE to one with the other bits zero, then within four cycles write the new CLKPS with CLKPCE zero, with interrupts off.

Six modes: Idle, ADC Noise Reduction, Power-down, Power-save, Standby and Extended Standby, chosen by SM2:0 in SMCR and entered by setting SE and executing SLEEP. An enabled interrupt wakes the MCU; it halts for four cycles plus the start-up time, runs the interrupt routine and continues after the SLEEP. Register file and SRAM keep their contents. A reset during sleep wakes the part to the reset vector.

On the ATmega48PA/88PA/168PA/328P, writing BODS in MCUCR (bit 6) through a timed sequence turns the brown-out detector off in Power-down, Power-save, Standby and Extended Standby, so the sleep current matches a part with the BOD fused off. It switches back on by itself at wake-up, and wake-up then takes about 60 µs so the BOD is working before code runs. BODS is zero by default.

SM2:0 = 000. The CPU and Flash clocks stop; SPI, USART, analog comparator, ADC, 2-wire interface, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so external and internal interrupts both wake the part. The comparator can be powered down with ACD in ACSR if not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

SM2:0 = 001. clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH stop; the ADC, external interrupts, TWI address watch, Timer/Counter2 (asynchronous only) and watchdog keep running. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, TWI address match, Timer/Counter2, SPM/EEPROM ready, INT0/INT1 level interrupt and pin change interrupt.

SM2:0 = 010. The external oscillator stops; only asynchronous modules run. External interrupts, TWI address watch and watchdog stay active. Wake-up sources: external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, TWI address match, INT0/INT1 level interrupt and pin change interrupt. A level interrupt must last until the start-up time ends or the part wakes without taking the interrupt. The wake-up delay is the same CKSEL-set start-up period used after reset.

SM2:0 = 011. Power-down, except that Timer/Counter2 keeps running and its overflow or compare match can wake the part when enabled in TIMSK2 with I set. Without Timer/Counter2 running, Power-down is the better choice. Whichever of the asynchronous and synchronous clocks the timer does not use is stopped; the synchronous clock, if running, reaches Timer/Counter2 only.

With an external crystal or resonator selected: SM2:0 = 110 gives Standby, Power-down with the oscillator kept running; SM2:0 = 111 gives Extended Standby, Power-save with the oscillator kept running. Both wake in six clock cycles.

Bits in PRR stop the clock to single peripherals in Active and Idle mode. A stopped module freezes, its registers cannot be read or written, and it keeps the resources it held, so disable it first. Clearing the bit restarts it as it was.

Turn off what is not used before sleeping. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode, and the next conversion after turning it back on is an extended one. Disable the analog comparator in Idle and ADC Noise Reduction, and in every mode if it uses the internal reference. A fuse-enabled BOD and an enabled watchdog run in every sleep mode and weigh heavily in deep sleep. The internal reference is on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and must settle after being turned on. With the DWEN fuse set, the main clock keeps running in sleep.

No pin should drive a resistive load in sleep. With both clkI/O and clkADC stopped the digital input buffers are off, except where needed for wake-up; an enabled buffer with a floating input or one near VCC/2 draws excess current. Analog inputs should always have their digital buffer disabled through DIDR0 and DIDR1, since a level near VCC/2 draws current even in active mode.

Reset returns every I/O register to its initial value and starts at the reset vector, which holds a JMP on the 168 and 328 devices and an RJMP on the 48 and 88. Unused interrupt vector space may hold ordinary code. The I/O ports go to their reset state at once, without a clock. When all reset sources have released, a delay counter set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Four: power-on reset while VCC is below VPOT; external reset from a low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse; watchdog system reset when the watchdog expires in reset mode; and brown-out reset while VCC is below VBOT with the detector enabled. MCUSR flags which source acted (PORF, BORF, EXTRF, WDRF).

An on-chip detector holds reset whenever VCC is below its level. Crossing it on the way up starts the delay counter; falling below it reasserts reset at once. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally to stretch the start.

A low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even without a clock; shorter pulses are not guaranteed to. When RESET rises through VRST the delay counter starts and the MCU runs after tTOUT. The RSTDISBL fuse disables it.

The BOD compares VCC with a trigger level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Below VBOT− brown-out reset asserts at once; above VBOT+ the delay counter starts and the MCU runs after tTOUT. A dip is seen only if VCC remains under the trigger level for more than tBOD.
On time-out the watchdog issues a one-clock reset pulse; its falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

A bandgap reference serves the BOD and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It is on while the BOD is fuse-enabled, while ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, and while the ADC is enabled. With the BOD off, allow its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using the result. Avoiding all three before Power-down turns it off.

Counts cycles of its own 128 kHz oscillator, with time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s chosen by WDP3:0 (2K to 1024K cycles). Three modes: interrupt (to wake from sleep or as a general timer), system reset (against runaway code), and interrupt then system reset (to save state before resetting). WDR restarts the count. The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode, locking WDE to 1 and WDIE to 0. Clearing WDE or changing the time-out takes a timed sequence: write WDCE and WDE to one together, then within four cycles write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE zero, in one operation. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, since a shorter period can expire at once.

A watchdog switched on by accident (a stray pointer or a brown-out) stays on through the reset it causes, and code that does not expect it resets endlessly. Startup code should clear WDRF in MCUSR and WDE even when the watchdog is unused.

Each vector is two instruction words on the 168 and 328 devices and one on the 48 and 88. The 48 devices have no boot section; on the 88, 168 and 328 the BOOTRST fuse moves the reset vector and IVSEL in MCUCR moves the interrupt vectors to the boot section. With a 2 Kbyte boot section the boot start is 0xC00 on the 88, 0x1C00 on the 168 and 0x3C00 on the 328 (word addresses). Where the reset vector and the interrupt vectors are in different sections, or no interrupt is ever enabled, the unused vector space can hold code.

INT0 and INT1 trigger on a falling edge, a rising edge or a low level, set in EICRA; a low-level interrupt repeats while the pin stays low. Low level and edge detection on INT0 and INT1 are asynchronous, so they can wake the part from any sleep mode; the I/O clock runs only in Idle. Enabled interrupts fire even when the pin is an output, which gives a way to raise a software interrupt.

PCI0 fires when any enabled pin of PCINT7:0 toggles, PCI1 for PCINT14:8 and PCI2 for PCINT23:16; PCMSK0, PCMSK1 and PCMSK2 choose the pins. Detection is asynchronous, so pin changes wake the part from sleep modes beyond Idle.

Every port supports read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, value or pull-up without disturbing the others. Outputs drive symmetrically with high sink and source current, enough for LED displays. Each pin has a selectable pull-up of supply-independent resistance and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three registers: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read only). PUD in MCUCR disables every pull-up. Turning on one pin's alternate function leaves the port's other pins free as I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, 0 an input. As an input, PORTxn = 1 turns the pull-up on and 0 turns it off. As an output, PORTxn drives the pin high or low. Pins are tri-stated while reset is active, clock or no clock. Writing a one to PINxn toggles PORTxn whatever DDxn holds.

Going from tri-state (00) to output high (11) passes through either pull-up on (01) or output low (10); the pull-up state is usually harmless, otherwise set PUD. From input with pull-up to output low, pass through tri-state or output high.

PINxn can be read whatever the direction. A latch and a flip-flop synchronise it, so an outside change reaches PINxn between half and one and a half system clocks later. Reading back a value the software just wrote needs one NOP between the OUT and the IN; the delay through the synchroniser is then one clock.

In Power-down, Power-save and Standby the sleep controller clamps the digital input to ground ahead of the Schmitt trigger, so floating or mid-supply inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and several alternate functions, override the clamp. An asynchronous interrupt pin set for any edge but not enabled, and held high, will have its flag set on wake-up because the clamp release looks like an edge.

Unused pins should have a defined level to save current in reset, active and Idle modes, where inputs are live. The internal pull-up is simplest but is off during reset; where reset current matters, fit an external resistor to either rail. Tying a pin straight to VCC or GND is not recommended, as it draws heavy current if the pin is ever set as an output.

A peripheral takes over a pin through override signals on its pull-up (PUOE/PUOV), direction (DDOE/DDOV), output value (PVOE/PVOV), toggle (PTOE) and digital input enable (DIEOE/DIEOV), and reads it through DI (digital, after the Schmitt trigger) or AIO (analog, straight from the pad).

XTAL1/XTAL2 serve every clock source but the internal calibrated RC; TOSC1/TOSC2 serve the asynchronous timer only with that RC clock and AS2 set (EXCLK clear for a crystal). A pin used for the clock is lost as I/O and its DDR, PORT and PIN bits read 0. The SPI forces SCK, MOSI and SS to inputs in slave mode and MISO to an input in master mode; otherwise the DDR bit sets direction, and a forced input still takes its pull-up from the PORT bit. As a slave, the SPI is active while SS is low. OC1A, OC1B and OC2A need the pin set as an output and also carry PWM. CLKO is driven when CKOUT is programmed, whatever PORTB0 and DDB0 hold, and during reset.

With RSTDISBL programmed PC6 is ordinary I/O and only power-on and brown-out resets remain; unprogrammed, it is RESET and reads 0 in DDC6, PORTC6 and PINC6. With TWEN set, PC4 and PC5 leave the port to become SDA and SCL with an open-drain, slew-limited driver and an input spike filter that suppresses pulses under 50 ns. ADC4 and ADC5 run from the digital supply; ADC0 to ADC3 from the analog supply.

For AIN0 and AIN1, set the pin as an input with the pull-up off so the port does not disturb the comparator. OC0A, OC0B and OC2B need the pin set as an output and also carry PWM; OC2B on PD3 is the Timer/Counter2 compare match B output. The enabled USART transmitter forces TXD to an output and the receiver forces RXD to an input, whose pull-up still follows PORTD0.

Timer/Counter0 is an 8-bit timer with two output compare units (A and B), double-buffered compare registers, clear-on-compare (auto reload), glitch-free phase correct PWM, variable PWM period and a frequency generator. It raises three interrupts: overflow TOV0 and compare matches OCF0A and OCF0B. It is enabled by writing PRTIM0 in the power reduction register to zero.

TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit. Interrupt flags sit in TIFR0 and masks in TIMSK0. The counter runs from the prescaled internal clock or an external clock on pin T0, chosen by CS02:0 in TCCR0B; with no clock selected (CS02:0 = 0) it stops, though the CPU can still read and write TCNT0. The selected clock is called clkT0. Both compare registers are compared with the counter all the time; a match can drive OC0A or OC0B and sets OCF0A or OCF0B.

The counter is cleared, counted up or counted down on each clkT0, as the mode chosen by WGM02:0 (WGM01:0 in TCCR0A, WGM02 in TCCR0B) requires. A CPU write to TCNT0 takes priority over any count or clear in the same cycle. TOV0 is set at a point that depends on the mode and can raise an interrupt.

When TCNT0 equals OCR0A or OCR0B the matching flag is set on the next timer clock; the flag clears when its interrupt runs, or when a one is written to it. In the PWM modes the compare registers are double buffered and update at TOP or BOTTOM, which keeps PWM pulses symmetrical and glitch-free; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes the compare register directly. In non-PWM modes writing FOC0x forces a match: the pin follows COM0x1:0 but no flag is set and the timer is not cleared.

Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can be set equal to TCNT0 without an interrupt. Writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x loses that match; writing BOTTOM while counting down should be avoided. Set OC0x before making the pin an output; FOC0x in Normal mode is the simplest way. OC0x keeps its value across mode changes. COM0x1:0 is not double buffered and acts at once.

COM0x1:0 chooses what OC0x does on the next match and also hands the pin to the waveform generator when either bit is set; the pin's DDR bit still sets direction and must be an output for OC0x to appear. A reset clears the internal OC0x register. COM0x1:0 = 0 means no action on a match. A new COM0x1:0 setting acts from the next compare match onward, or at once in non-PWM modes with FOC0x.

WGM02:0 = 0. The counter only counts up and wraps from 0xFF to 0x00; TOV0 is set in the clock that TCNT0 becomes zero, acting like a ninth bit that software can extend through the overflow interrupt. A new count can be written at any time. Compare units can time interrupts; making waveforms in this mode takes too much CPU time and is not recommended.

WGM02:0 = 2. The counter clears when TCNT0 matches OCR0A, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution. OCF0A can interrupt at each TOP. CTC is not double buffered: writing an OCR0A value below the current count while running fast misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFF and wraps first. With COM0A1:0 = 1 OC0A toggles each match, reaching fclk_I/O/2 at OCR0A = 0. TOV0 is set when the count passes MAX to 0x00.

WGM02:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A). Single slope: count BOTTOM to TOP, clear on the next clock. Non-inverting (COM0x1:0 = 2) clears OC0x on match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting (3) does the opposite. It runs at up to twice the frequency of phase correct PWM, which suits power regulation, rectification and DAC use with small external parts. TOV0 is set at TOP. With WGM02 set, COM0A1:0 = 1 toggles OC0A on each match (not available on OC0B), giving a 50 % square wave up to fclk_I/O/2 with the compare register double buffered. OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR0A at MAX gives a steady high or low.

WGM02:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A). Dual slope: count BOTTOM to TOP and back, holding TOP for one clock. Non-inverting clears OC0x on the up-count match and sets it on the down-count match. Its symmetry suits motor control; its top frequency is lower than fast PWM. TOV0 is set at BOTTOM. With WGM02 set, COM0A0 = 1 toggles OC0A on match (not OC0B). OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a steady low and at MAX a steady high (non-inverted). OC0x can also change at BOTTOM with no match, to keep the waveform symmetrical: when OCR0x changes from MAX, and when the timer starts above OCR0x and misses the up-count match.

The timer is synchronous; clkT0 acts as a clock enable. TOV0 is set as the count goes from MAX to BOTTOM; OCF0x is set on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x; in CTC and fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, OCF0A is set and TCNT0 cleared as the count passes TOP.

Timer/Counter1 is a true 16-bit timer (16-bit PWM is possible) with two output compare units, double-buffered compare registers, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM, variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter. It raises four interrupts: TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B and ICF1. It is enabled by writing PRTIM1 in PRR to zero. Its pins are T1, ICP1, OC1A and OC1B.

TCNT1, OCR1A, OCR1B and ICR1 are 16-bit; TCCR1A and TCCR1B are 8-bit with no access restriction. Flags sit in TIFR1 and masks in TIMSK1. The clock is the prescaler or pin T1; the selected clock is clkT1. ICR1 captures the count on an edge at ICP1 or at the analog comparator output, through a digital noise filter. TOP can be a fixed value, OCR1A or ICR1. With OCR1A as TOP in a PWM mode, OCR1A gives no PWM output but TOP is double buffered and can change while running; ICR1 as TOP leaves OCR1A free for PWM.

The 16-bit registers are reached over the 8-bit bus in two accesses through one shared temporary high-byte register per timer. Writing the low byte copies the temporary high byte and the low byte into the register in one clock; reading the low byte copies the high byte into the temporary register. Write the high byte first; read the low byte first. Reading OCR1A/B does not use the temporary register. C compilers handle the order. If an interrupt routine also touches any 16-bit timer register, the main code must disable interrupts around its own 16-bit access, or the result is corrupted. When several registers share the same high byte, it need be written only once, under the same rule.

TCNT1 is mapped as TCNT1H and TCNT1L; the CPU reaches TCNT1H only through the temporary register, which loads from TCNT1H when TCNT1L is read and is written to TCNT1H when TCNT1L is written, so the whole count moves in one clock. Some writes to TCNT1 while counting give unpredictable results. The count is cleared, incremented or decremented per clkT1 as WGM13:0 (in TCCR1A and TCCR1B) requires; CS12:0 = 0 stops the timer, and a CPU write takes priority over counting. TOV1 is set according to the mode.

An event on ICP1, or on the analog comparator output (ACO) when ACIC in ACSR is set, that matches the chosen edge copies TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1 in the same clock; with ICIE1 set this interrupts, and ICF1 clears when the interrupt runs or when a one is written to it. Read ICR1L before ICR1H. ICR1 can be written only in a mode that uses it as TOP, after WGM13:0 is set, high byte first. Changing the trigger source can cause a capture, so clear ICF1 after the change. ICP1 and ACO are sampled like pin T1 with the same edge detector. The noise canceler and edge detector input stay enabled unless ICR1 sets TOP. A capture can be caused from software by driving the ICP1 port bit.

With ICNC1 in TCCR1B set, the input must read the same on four successive samples before the edge detector sees a change. This adds four system clocks of delay before ICR1 updates; it runs on the system clock and is not prescaled.

ICR1 must be read before the next event or it is overwritten; read it early in the interrupt routine, and allow for the longest time any other interrupt can take. Changing TOP while capturing is not recommended. To measure duty cycle, change the edge right after reading ICR1 and then clear ICF1 by writing a one; to measure frequency only, clearing ICF1 is not needed when an interrupt is used. In Normal mode the interval between events must fit in the counter's range, extended with the overflow interrupt or the prescaler if needed.

TCNT1 is compared with OCR1A and OCR1B all the time; a match sets OCF1x on the next timer clock and, with OCIE1x set, interrupts. Unit A can also set TOP, which fixes the period. OCR1x is double buffered in the twelve PWM modes and written directly in Normal and CTC. OCR1x changes only when written, so it is read without the temporary register (reading low byte first is still good practice), but it is written through it, high byte first. FOC1x forces a match in non-PWM modes without setting the flag or clearing the timer.

A CPU write to TCNT1 blocks a match in the next timer clock, even when stopped. Writing TCNT1 equal to OCR1x loses that match. In PWM modes with variable TOP, writing TCNT1 equal to TOP loses the TOP match and the counter runs on to 0xFFFF. Avoid writing BOTTOM while counting down. Set OC1x before making the pin an output; OC1x keeps its value across modes; COM1x1:0 is not double buffered and acts at once.

COM1x1:0 sets what OC1x does on the next match and gives the pin to the waveform generator when either bit is set; the DDR bit must make the pin an output. The override is mostly independent of the mode, with exceptions listed in the compare output tables. A reset clears OC1x. COM1x1:0 does not affect the input capture unit. A change takes effect at the next match, or at once in non-PWM modes with FOC1x.

WGM13:0 = 0. Count up only, wrap from 0xFFFF to 0x0000; TOV1 is set as TCNT1 becomes zero and acts as a 17th bit. A new count can be written at any time. Waveforms from this mode cost too much CPU time and are not recommended.

WGM13:0 = 4 (TOP = OCR1A) or 12 (TOP = ICR1). The counter clears on matching TOP; OCF1A or ICF1 can interrupt there. Not double buffered: an OCR1A or ICR1 value written below the current count misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFFFF and wraps first; fast PWM with OCR1A as TOP (mode 15) avoids this through its double buffer. COM1A1:0 = 1 toggles OC1A each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0. TOV1 is set when the count passes MAX to 0x0000.

WGM13:0 = 5, 6, 7 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF), 14 (TOP = ICR1) or 15 (TOP = OCR1A). Single slope, up to twice the frequency of the dual-slope modes. Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOV1 is set at TOP, and OCF1A or ICF1 in the same clock when that register is TOP. A new TOP must be at least every compare value, or those matches never happen; with fixed TOP, unused bits of OCR1x are masked to zero on write. ICR1 is not double buffered, so a low value written while running fast can miss TOP and wrap through 0xFFFF; OCR1A is double buffered and loads from its buffer at TOP as TCNT1 clears and TOV1 sets. ICR1 as TOP suits a fixed period with OCR1A free for PWM; OCR1A as TOP suits a period that changes. COM1x1:0 = 2 is non-inverting, 3 inverting. OCR1x at BOTTOM gives a spike every TOP+1 clocks and at TOP a steady level. In mode 15 COM1A1:0 = 1 toggles OC1A for a 50 % square wave up to fclk_I/O/2.

WGM13:0 = 1, 2, 3 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF), 10 (TOP = ICR1) or 11 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual slope; resolution 2 to 16 bits as in fast PWM; TCNT1 holds TOP for one clock. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM; OCF1A or ICF1 is set at TOP as the compare registers load from their buffers. Because the registers update at TOP, changing TOP while running makes a period asymmetrical (the falling slope uses the old TOP, the rising the new); phase and frequency correct mode is recommended when TOP changes, and with a fixed TOP the two modes are practically the same. OCR1x at BOTTOM gives a steady low and at TOP a steady high (non-inverted). In mode 11 with COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50 % duty.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGM13:0 = 8 (TOP = ICR1) or 9 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual slope; the compare registers load from their buffers at BOTTOM, so the two slopes of each period are always equal and every period is symmetrical. Resolution 2 to 16 bits. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM as the registers update; OCF1A or ICF1 is set at TOP. TOP must stay at or above every compare value. OCR1x at BOTTOM gives a steady low and at TOP a high (non-inverted). In mode 9 with COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50 % duty.

clkT1 acts as a clock enable. OCF1x is set on the timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x. In CTC and fast PWM the count goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the dual-slope modes it turns at TOP. TOV1 (fast PWM) and ICF1 (when ICR1 is TOP) are set as the count leaves TOP, where double-buffered OCR1x also updates; in phase and frequency correct mode the update happens at BOTTOM instead, as for modes that set TOV1 at BOTTOM.

Timer/Counter0 and Timer/Counter1 share one free-running prescaler but choose their settings separately. CSn2:0 = 1 clocks the timer at the system clock fclk_I/O, the fastest rate; the prescaler taps give fclk_I/O/8, /64, /256 and /1024. Because the prescaler runs regardless of the timer's clock select, the first count after enabling a prescaled timer comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later (N = 8, 64, 256 or 1024). Resetting the prescaler (PSRSYNC) can align a timer to program flow, but it resets the period for both timers.

operation.topic: External clock on T0 and T1
operation.text: Pin T0 or T1 is sampled every system clock, synchronised and edge-detected; CSn2:0 = 7 counts rising edges and 6 falling edges. The path delays the count by 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks. Enable or disable the input only after the pin has held steady for a system clock or more, or a false count may occur. Each half period must exceed one system clock: below fclk_I/O/2 at 50 % duty, and below fclk_I/O/2.5 recommended to allow for oscillator tolerance. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

Timer/Counter2 is an 8-bit timer with clear-on-compare, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a frequency generator and a 10-bit prescaler. It raises TOV2, OCF2A and OCF2B, and can run from an external 32 kHz watch crystal independently of the I/O clock. It is enabled by writing PRTIM2 to zero.

TCNT2, OCR2A and OCR2B are 8-bit; flags are in TIFR2 and masks in TIMSK2. The clock is the I/O clock through the prescaler by default, or, with AS2 in ASSR set, the Timer/Counter oscillator on TOSC1 and TOSC2. The selected clock is clkT2; with none selected (CS22:0 = 0) the timer stops. Counting follows WGM22:0 (WGM21:0 in TCCR2A, WGM22 in TCCR2B). Compare units, forced compare, compare blocking on a TCNT2 write, the compare output unit and the Normal, CTC, fast PWM and phase correct PWM modes behave as in Timer/Counter0, with TOP fixed at 0xFF or set by OCR2A.

A match of TCNT2 with OCR2A or OCR2B sets OCF2x on the next timer clock and can interrupt; the flag clears when serviced or when a one is written. OCR2x is double buffered in PWM modes and direct in Normal and CTC. FOC2x forces a match in non-PWM modes without setting the flag. A TCNT2 write blocks a match in the next timer clock; writing TCNT2 equal to OCR2x loses the match. Set OC2x before making the pin an output. COM2x1:0 is not double buffered and acts at once.

Normal (WGM22:0 = 0): count up, wrap at 0xFF, TOV2 at zero. CTC (2): clear at OCR2A, no double buffer, OC2A toggle up to fclk_I/O/2. Fast PWM (3: TOP = 0xFF; 7: TOP = OCR2A): single slope, TOV2 at TOP; COM2x1:0 = 2 non-inverting, 3 inverting; OCR2A at BOTTOM gives a spike every MAX+1 clocks and at MAX a steady level; COM2x1:0 = 1 gives a 50 % toggle up to fclk_I/O/2 with double buffering. Phase correct PWM (1: TOP = 0xFF; 5: TOP = OCR2A): dual slope, TOV2 at BOTTOM; OCR2A at BOTTOM steady low, at MAX steady high (non-inverted); OC2x may change at BOTTOM without a match when OCR2A leaves MAX or the timer starts above OCR2A. Timer/Counter2's prescale factor N is 1, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256 or 1024.

In synchronous mode clkT2 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O; in asynchronous mode the oscillator clock takes the place of clkI/O. TOV2 sets as the count passes MAX to BOTTOM, OCF2x on the timer clock after a match, and in CTC OCF2A sets and TCNT2 clears as the count passes TOP.

operation.topic: Switching Timer/Counter2 between synchronous and asynchronous clocks
operation.text: Changing AS2 can corrupt TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x. Safe order: clear OCIE2x and TOIE2; set AS2 as wanted; write TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x; when going asynchronous, wait for TCN2UB, OCR2xUB and TCR2xUB to clear; clear the Timer/Counter2 interrupt flags; turn the interrupts back on as required. In asynchronous mode the CPU clock has to exceed the timer oscillator frequency by more than a factor of four.

In asynchronous mode a write to TCNT2, OCR2x or TCCR2x goes to that register's own temporary register and is latched after two rising edges on TOSC1; ASSR's update-busy flags show when each transfer is done, and a register should not be written again until it is. Before entering Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction with Timer/Counter2 as the wake-up source, wait for the written register to update: compare is disabled while OCR2x or TCNT2 is being written, and sleeping before OCR2xUB clears means the compare interrupt never comes and the part never wakes. Re-entering sleep within the same TOSC1 cycle as a wake-up interrupt wakes it again at once; to be sure one TOSC1 cycle has passed, write TCCR2x, TCNT2 or OCR2x, wait for its busy flag to clear, then sleep.

With asynchronous operation selected, the 32.768 kHz oscillator runs in every mode except Power-down and Standby. After power-up or wake from Power-down or Standby it can take up to one second to settle; wait at least one second before using Timer/Counter2, and treat all its registers as lost after such a wake, whether a crystal or an external clock on TOSC1 is used. On wake from Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction the timer has advanced at least one count before the CPU can read it; the MCU halts four cycles, runs the interrupt, then continues after the SLEEP instruction.

TCNT2 is read through a register synchronised to the I/O clock on each rising TOSC1 edge, so just after waking from Power-save it reads the value from before sleep until the next TOSC1 rising edge, whose phase is unpredictable. To read it correctly: write any value to OCR2x or TCCR2x, wait for that busy flag to clear, then read TCNT2. Interrupt flags of the asynchronous timer take three CPU cycles plus one timer cycle to synchronise. The compare output pin changes on the timer clock, not synchronised to the CPU clock.

Timer/Counter2's clock source clkT2S is the I/O clock, or with AS2 set the TOSC1 pin, which makes the timer a real-time counter. With AS2 set, TOSC1 and TOSC2 leave Port B and a crystal between them clocks the timer; the oscillator is optimised for 32.768 kHz. CS22:0 selects stop, clkT2S, or clkT2S/8, /32, /64, /128, /256 or /1024. Setting PSRASY in GTCCR resets the prescaler so its phase is known.

The SPI is a full-duplex three-wire synchronous port, master or slave, LSB or MSB first, with seven bit rates, an end-of-transfer interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake-up from Idle and a double-speed (CK/2) master mode. The clock divider offers /2, /4, /8, /16, /32, /64 and /128. The USART can also act as an SPI master. It is enabled by writing PRSPI to zero.

The master starts a transfer by pulling the chosen slave's SS low; both load their shift registers and the master clocks SCK, data moving master to slave on MOSI and slave to master on MISO; the master raises SS after each packet. As master the SPI does not drive SS itself: software does, then a write to SPDR starts eight clocks, after which SPIF is set (and an interrupt requested if SPIE is set). As slave it sleeps with MISO tri-stated while SS is high; SPDR may be loaded but shifts only once SS is low. The last received byte stays in the buffer register.

operation.topic: SPI buffering and slave clock limits
operation.text: Transmit is single buffered: a new byte cannot be written to SPDR until the shift is complete. Receive is double buffered: a byte must be read before the next one has fully shifted in, or the first is lost. In slave mode SCK low and high periods must each be longer than 2 CPU clock cycles. Enabling the SPI overrides the direction of MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS.

As a slave SS is always an input. SS low activates the SPI and MISO is an output if so set; SS high makes every pin an input, the SPI ignores incoming data, and the send and receive logic reset at once, dropping any partly received byte. This keeps the slave's bit counter in step with the master.

With MSTR set, SS as an output is a plain output that does not affect the SPI, typically driving the slave's SS. SS as an input must be held high for master operation; if it is pulled low, the SPI takes it as another master selecting it: MSTR clears, MOSI and SCK become inputs, SPIF sets and the interrupt runs if enabled. Interrupt-driven masters should check MSTR is still set and set it again if needed.
CPOL and CPHA give four combinations of clock polarity and phase; data is shifted out and latched in on opposite SCK edges so it has time to settle. DORD = 0 sends MSB first, DORD = 1 LSB first.

USART0 is a full-duplex serial port with separate receive and transmit registers, asynchronous or synchronous (master or slave clocked), with a high-resolution baud rate generator; frames of 5 to 9 data bits and 1 or 2 stop bits; hardware odd or even parity; overrun and framing error detection; noise filtering with false start bit detection and a digital low-pass filter; three interrupts (receive done, transmit done, transmit buffer empty); a multi-processor mode; and double-speed asynchronous operation. It can also be an SPI master. It is enabled by writing PRUSART0 to zero. It has a clock generator, a transmitter with one write buffer (frames follow each other with no gap) and a receiver with clock and data recovery, parity checker and a receive buffer UDRn two characters deep; it detects frame, overrun and parity errors. XCKn is used only in synchronous mode.

Clocking is asynchronous at normal or double speed, or synchronous with the USART as clock master or clock slave. UMSELn in UCSRnC picks asynchronous or synchronous; U2Xn in UCSRnA sets double speed (asynchronous only); in synchronous mode the DDR bit of XCKn picks internal clock (master, output) or external (slave, input).

UBRRn loads a down-counter running at fosc each time it reaches zero or UBRRnL is written; each zero gives one baud generator clock, fosc/(UBRRn+1). The transmitter divides this by 2, 8 or 16 by mode; the receiver's recovery units use it directly with a 2, 8 or 16 state machine set by UMSELn, U2Xn and DDR_XCKn. UBRRn spans 0 to 4095.

U2Xn = 1 halves the baud divider from 16 to 8 and doubles the asynchronous rate; it has no effect in synchronous mode and should then be zero. The receiver then takes 8 samples per bit instead of 16, so baud rate and system clock must be more accurate; the transmitter is unaffected.

In synchronous slave mode XCKn is passed through a synchronisation register and an edge detector, adding two CPU clocks of delay, which limits XCKn to below fosc/4. Margin is recommended since fosc varies with its source.

With UMSELn = 1 XCKn is the clock input (slave) or output (master). Data on RxDn is sampled on the XCKn edge opposite to the one on which TxDn changes: UCPOLn = 0 changes data on the rising edge and samples on the falling; UCPOLn = 1 changes on the falling and samples on the rising.

A frame is one start bit (low), 5 to 9 data bits LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit, and 1 or 2 stop bits (high); 30 combinations are valid. A frame may follow at once or the line may idle high. UCSZn2:0 sets the data bits, UPMn1:0 the parity and USBSn the stop bits, shared by receiver and transmitter; changing them corrupts any transfer in progress. The receiver ignores the second stop bit, so a frame error is flagged only when the first stop bit is zero.

Set the baud rate, set the frame format and enable the transmitter and/or receiver; with interrupt-driven use, disable interrupts globally during setup. Before changing baud rate or format, make sure no transfer is in progress: TXCn shows the transmitter has finished (clear it before each UDRn write if used this way) and RXCn shows unread data.

TXENn in UCSRnB enables the transmitter and takes over TxDn; in synchronous mode XCKn is the transmit clock. Writing UDRn loads the transmit buffer, which moves to the shift register when it is idle or right after the previous frame's last stop bit. In frames under 8 bits the unused high bits of UDRn are ignored. For 9-bit frames (UCSZn = 7) write the ninth bit to TXB8n before the low byte to UDRn; the ninth bit can mark an address frame in multi-processor mode.

UDREn is set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing UDRn; with UDRIEn set its interrupt repeats while UDREn is set, so the routine must write UDRn or disable the interrupt. Write UDREn as zero when writing UCSRnA. TXCn is set when the whole frame has shifted out and the buffer is empty; it clears when its interrupt (TXCIEn) runs or when a one is written. TXCn suits half-duplex links such as RS-485, where the transmitter must release the bus as soon as it finishes. With parity on (UPMn1 = 1) the parity bit sits after the final data bit, ahead of the stop bits. Clearing TXENn takes effect only after pending transmissions finish; the pin is then released.

RXENn enables the receiver and takes over RxDn; in synchronous mode XCKn is the clock. Reception starts at a valid start bit; bits are shifted in up to the first stop bit (a second one is ignored) and the frame moves to the receive buffer, read from UDRn. Unused high bits of short frames read as zero. For 9-bit frames read RXB8n from UCSRnB first, and read the status bits FEn, DORn and UPEn from UCSRnA before UDRn, since reading UDRn advances the buffer they are stored with.

operation.topic: USART0 receive complete and error flags
operation.text: RXCn is set while unread data is in the receive buffer; disabling the receiver flushes it. With RXCIEn set the interrupt repeats until UDRn is read. FEn is set when the frame now at the head of the buffer had a zero in its first stop bit, useful for out-of-sync and break detection; it ignores USBSn. DORn shows one or more frames were lost because the two-character buffer was full, a character waited in the shift register and a new start bit came; it clears when a frame moves into the buffer. UPEn shows the next frame had a parity error when checking was on (UPMn1 = 1, UPMn0 picks odd or even), and is valid until UDRn is read. The error flags cannot be written by software, raise no interrupts, and should be written as zero.

operation.topic: USART0 disabling and flushing the receiver
operation.text: Disabling the receiver acts at once: a frame in progress is lost, RxDn is released and the buffer is flushed. To flush during operation, read UDRn until RXCn clears.

Clock recovery samples RxDn at 16 times the baud rate (8 in double speed). A high-to-low edge starts start bit detection; counting the first low sample as 1, samples 8, 9 and 10 (4, 5 and 6 in double speed) are voted, and if two or more are high the edge is rejected as a noise spike. A valid start bit resynchronises the clock; this repeats every start bit.

Each bit is decided by majority vote of the three centre samples of its 16 (or 8) states, which acts as a low-pass filter. The stop bit is voted the same way; a zero sets FEn. In normal speed the next start bit may begin right after the last voting sample of the stop bit; in double speed its first low sample must come later. How early a start bit is accepted affects the receiver's operating range.

The receiver tolerates only a limited mismatch between the incoming bit rate and its own baud rate. Normal speed tolerates more variation than double speed. The recommended limits assume the receiver and transmitter share the total error equally. Receiver error comes from the system clock (rarely a problem with a crystal, but a resonator may be more than 2 % off) and from the baud generator's inexact division, which is chosen for low error.

MPCMn in UCSRnA makes the receiver discard frames that are not address frames. With 5 to 8 data bits the first stop bit marks the frame type; with 9 data bits RXB8n does: one is an address, zero is data. The master sends 9-bit frames with TXB8n = 1 for an address and 0 for data; slaves use 9-bit frames too. Procedure: every slave sets MPCMn; the master sends an address frame, which every slave receives; each slave reads it and, if addressed, clears MPCMn, otherwise keeps it set; the addressed slave receives data frames while the rest ignore them; after its last data frame it sets MPCMn again and waits. 5 to 8 bit frames are possible but impractical, as the receiver must switch between n and n+1 bit frames, and the transmitter must then use two stop bits. Do not use SBI or CBI on MPCMn: it shares an I/O location with TXCn, which they can clear by accident.

For common crystal and resonator frequencies, UBRRn settings within 0.5 % of a standard baud rate are available up to a limit that depends on the frequency. Errors above 0.5 % are acceptable but leave the receiver less noise margin, especially with long frames.

Setting both UMSELn1:0 bits puts the USART into master SPI mode: full duplex three-wire transfer, master only, all four SPI modes, LSB or MSB first, double-buffered queued operation, the high-resolution baud generator, speeds up to fXCKmax = fCK/2, and flexible interrupts. The SPI logic takes over the shift registers, buffers and baud generator; parity, clock and data recovery and the RX/TX control logic are off. Pin control, interrupt generation and register addresses stay as in USART mode, though some control bits change meaning.

Only the internal clock (master) is supported, so XCKn's DDR bit must be set as an output, preferably before TXENn and RXENn are set. The clock is generated as in synchronous master mode, so the same baud equations apply.

UCPOLn and UCPHAn give the four clock polarity and phase combinations; data shifts out and in on opposite XCKn edges. A frame is 8 data bits, MSB or LSB first as UDORDn sets; the line idles high between frames. Changing these bits corrupts transfers in progress. A 16-bit transfer is two bytes written to UDRn, with the transmit complete interrupt marking the end.

Set the baud rate, make XCKn an output (master), set the frame format and enable transmitter and receiver; only the transmitter can work alone. For XCKn to start at once, UBRRn must be zero when the transmitter is enabled and be written with the wanted value afterwards, before the first transfer; straight after reset UBRRn is already zero. Before changing baud rate, data mode or format, check with TXCn and RXCn that nothing is in progress.

The transmitter must be enabled (TXENn), taking over TxDn; the receiver (RXENn, RxDn) is optional; XCKn is the clock. Writing UDRn starts every transfer, sending and receiving alike. Read UDRn once for each byte sent to keep the receive buffer in step: on overflow the newest byte is lost, so with four bytes sent and none read, byte 3 is the one lost. RXCn, TXCn and UDREn work as in USART mode; FE, DOR and PE always read zero. Disabling transmitter or receiver works as in USART mode.

The USART in MSPIM matches the SPI's master timing, and UCPOLn, UCPHAn and UDORDn act as CPOL, CPHA and DORD. It differs in being master only, with a double-buffered transmitter (the SPI has none), an extra receive buffer level, no write collision bit, no SPI2X bit (UBRRn gives the same result), incompatible interrupt timing and different pin control.

The 2-wire serial interface (TWI) is an I2C-compatible bus port needing only two lines: master and slave operation, transmitter or receiver, 7-bit addressing for up to 128 slaves, multi-master arbitration, transfers up to 400 kHz, slew-rate limited output drivers, spike suppression on the bus inputs, a fully programmable slave address with general call, and wake from sleep on address match. It is enabled by writing PRTWI to zero.

Up to 128 devices share a clock line SCL and a data line SDA, both bidirectional; the only external parts needed are one pull-up resistor from each line to the supply. Every device has its own address, and the protocol resolves contention.

All bus drivers are open-drain or open-collector, giving a wired-AND: a line is low when any device drives zero and is pulled high when all release it. Every AVR on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited only by the 400 pF bus capacitance limit and the 7-bit address space. The bus electrical limits are given separately for speeds below 100 kHz and up to 400 kHz.

Each data bit comes with one SCL pulse, and SDA must be stable while SCL is high, except for START and STOP. The master begins a transfer with START (SDA falls while SCL is high) and ends it with STOP (SDA rises while SCL is high); the bus is busy in between. A START sent before STOP is a REPEATED START, which starts a new transfer without giving up the bus; it behaves as a START.

An address packet is 9 bits: 7 address bits MSB first, a READ/WRITE bit (1 = read) and an acknowledge bit. An addressed slave pulls SDA low in the ninth clock (ACK); a busy slave leaves it high, after which the master may send STOP or REPEATED START. SLA+R and SLA+W name the address with read or write. Address 0000 000 is the general call: slaves set to accept it all ACK and take the following data; a general call with the read bit is meaningless. Addresses 1111 xxx are reserved.

A data packet is a byte MSB first plus an acknowledge bit. The master drives the clock, START and STOP; the receiver ACKs by pulling SDA low in the ninth clock, and sends a NACK after the last byte it wants or can take. A transmission is a START, the address packet, at least one data packet, and a STOP; START followed directly by STOP is illegal. A slave may hold SCL low to stretch the low period when the master is too fast or it needs time; the high period stays the master's, so the effective rate drops.

Several masters may start at once. The wired-AND of their SCL outputs gives a combined clock whose high time is the shortest master high time and whose low time is the longest master low time; every master times its high and low periods from the combined line. A master that loses arbitration must switch at once to slave mode in case the winner is addressing it, and the slaves must see no corruption.

Each master reads SDA after driving it; a master that drove high but reads low has lost and must stop driving SDA, though it may keep clocking to the end of the current packet, and should check whether it is being addressed. Arbitration may run over many bits and into the data when masters address the same slave. Arbitration between a REPEATED START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a REPEATED START and a STOP is not allowed; software must prevent it, so in a multi-master system every transfer must be built alike, with the same number of data packets after SLA+R/W, or the outcome is undefined.

The pin drivers have a slew-rate limiter to meet the TWI specification, and the inputs remove spikes shorter than 50 ns. The pad's internal pull-ups can be switched on by setting the PORT bits of SCL and SDA, and in some systems can replace external pull-ups.

In master modes the SCL period is set by TWBR and the prescaler bits in TWSR. Slave operation does not depend on these, but a slave's CPU clock must be at least 16 times the SCL frequency. Slaves stretching SCL low lower the average bus clock. Pull-up values are chosen from the SCL frequency and bus capacitance.

TWDR holds the address or data byte to send or just received. A hidden (N)ACK register holds the acknowledge bit: when receiving it is set through TWCR; when transmitting the received value shows in TWSR. The START/STOP controller generates and detects START, REPEATED START and STOP, and detects them even in sleep modes so an addressed part can wake. Arbitration detection watches transmissions the TWI started as master and reports a loss.

Received addresses are compared with the 7-bit address in TWAR, and with the general call address when TWGCE in TWAR is set. Whether the TWI acknowledges depends on TWCR. Comparison works in sleep, so a matching address wakes the MCU.

When a bus event needs the application, TWINT is set and TWSR takes a status code on the next clock; at other times TWSR holds a code meaning no information. SCL is held low while TWINT is set. TWINT is set after a START or REPEATED START is sent, after SLA+R/W is sent, after an address byte is sent, after arbitration is lost, after being addressed by own address or general call, after a data byte is received, after a STOP or REPEATED START is received while still addressed as slave, and on a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI is byte-oriented and interrupt-based, so software runs during each byte. TWIE in TWCR with the global interrupt bit decides whether TWINT raises an interrupt; otherwise software polls TWINT. On TWINT, TWSR gives the bus state, and software sets up TWDR and TWCR for the next bus cycle, then writes TWCR with TWINT set: writing a one clears TWINT and starts the operation, and nothing starts while it is set. A single-byte master write runs: write TWCR to send START; on TWINT check TWSR for START sent; load SLA+W into TWDR and write TWCR (TWINT one, TWSTA zero); on TWINT check for SLA+W sent and ACK; load the data byte and write TWCR; on TWINT check for data sent and ACK; write TWCR to send STOP. TWINT is not set after a STOP is sent.

The TWI works in four modes, MT and MR as a master sending or receiving, ST and SR as a slave sending or receiving; one application can use several, for example MT to write a TWI EEPROM and MR to read it back, and SR when other masters send to it. Each TWINT event leaves a status code in TWSR, read with the prescaler bits masked to zero; the transfer waits until software clears TWINT.

A master mode is entered by sending START; sending SLA+W then selects MT and SLA+R selects MR. After START, TWSR is 0x08; load SLA+W into TWDR and clear TWINT. After the address and acknowledge, TWSR is 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38. Data bytes are written to TWDR only while TWINT is high, otherwise the write is discarded and TWWC is set; each is followed by clearing TWINT. The transfer ends with STOP or a REPEATED START (state 0x10), which can reach the same or another slave, or switch between MT and MR, without giving up the bus.

Send START (TWSR 0x08), load SLA+R and clear TWINT; after the address TWSR is 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48. Each received byte is read from TWDR while TWINT is set. The master sends NACK after the last byte it wants, then STOP or REPEATED START.

Load TWAR with the own 7-bit address in the upper bits, with the LSB set to answer the general call (0x00); write TWCR with TWEN and TWEA set and TWSTA and TWSTO clear. The TWI then waits for its address (or general call) and direction bit: write enters SR, read enters ST. SR can also be entered after losing arbitration as master (states 0x68 and 0x78). Clearing TWEA during a transfer returns NACK after the next byte; while TWEA is zero the own address is not acknowledged but the bus is still watched, so TWEA can isolate the TWI for a while.

operation.topic: TWI wake-up from sleep as slave
operation.text: In every sleep mode except Idle the TWI clock is off, but with TWEA set it can still answer its own address or the general call, clocked by SCL itself. The part then wakes and holds SCL low until TWINT is cleared; reception or transmission continues normally with the clocks running. A long start-up time can hold SCL low for long and block other traffic. After waking from these modes TWDR does not hold the last byte on the bus.

Set up TWAR and TWCR as for SR; a read bit after the own address enters ST, as can losing arbitration as master (state 0xB0). If TWEA is cleared during a transfer, the TWI sends its last byte and enters 0xC0 or 0xC8 depending on whether the master answers NACK or ACK, then becomes a not-addressed slave and ignores the master, which then reads all ones. 0xC8 means the master asked for more after the last byte.

operation.topic: TWI miscellaneous states and bus error
operation.text: 0xF8 means no relevant information: TWINT is not set, between states or when the TWI is idle. 0x00 is a bus error: START or STOP at an illegal position, such as inside an address byte, data byte or acknowledge bit; TWINT is set. To recover, set TWSTO and clear TWINT by writing a one: the TWI becomes a not-addressed slave, clears TWSTO (no other TWCR bit changes), and releases SDA and SCL without sending STOP.

Reading a serial EEPROM uses MT to send the location and MR to read data. The master must keep the bus through both steps, so that in a multi-master system no other master moves the EEPROM's pointer in between; it does this with a REPEATED START between sending the address and receiving the data, so the sequence is START, address with write, the location byte, REPEATED START, address with read, the data answered with NACK, then STOP, each byte but the last acknowledged.

Masters doing identical transfers to the same slave never notice the contention. Masters sending the one slave differing data or a differing R/W bit lose arbitration in the R/W bit or the data where one drives a one against another's zero; losers become not-addressed slaves or wait for a free bus and send START, as software chooses. Masters addressing different slaves arbitrate in the SLA bits; losers switch to slave mode, enter SR or ST if addressed by the winner, or otherwise become not-addressed slaves or wait to send START. Arbitration lost in SLA or data gives status 0x38 if not addressed, 0x68 or 0x78 if addressed for write, and 0xB0 if addressed for read.

The comparator weighs AIN0 (positive input) against AIN1 (negative input) and sets its output ACO while AIN0 is the higher of the two. Its output can drive the Timer/Counter1 input capture, and it has an interrupt of its own that fires on a rising edge, a falling edge or either edge of the output. Using the ADC multiplexer as the comparator's input needs the PRADC power reduction bit at zero.

Any of ADC7...0 can stand in for AIN1. This works only with the ADC turned off: with ACME (ADCSRB) set and ADEN (ADCSRA) clear, the MUX2...0 bits of ADMUX pick the pin. With ACME clear or ADEN set, AIN1 is the negative input.

Setting ACD cuts power to the comparator, saving current in Active and Idle mode; clear ACIE before changing ACD or the change itself may raise an interrupt. ACBG swaps AIN0 for the internal bandgap reference, which needs time to settle before its first result is trustworthy. ACO is the output after a synchroniser that delays it by 1 to 2 clock cycles. ACI is set by the selected output event, cleared when the interrupt vector runs or by writing one to it.

A 10-bit successive approximation converter with a sample and hold, fed by an 8-channel single-ended multiplexer referred to GND (ADC6 and ADC7 exist on the TQFP and VQFN packages only), plus a temperature sensor channel. Figures given: integral non-linearity 0.5 LSB, absolute accuracy ±2 LSB, 13 µs to 260 µs per conversion, up to 76.9 kSPS (15 kSPS at full resolution), input range 0 V to VCC, a selectable 1.1 V reference, free running or single conversion, a conversion complete interrupt and a sleep mode noise canceler. The ADC has its own supply pin AVCC, which must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. References are the internal 1.1 V, AVCC, or a voltage on AREF; AREF can carry a capacitor to decouple the internal reference. PRADC must be zero for the ADC to run. Code 0 stands for GND and the top code for AREF less 1 LSB.

The MUX bits of ADMUX choose an input pin, GND or the fixed bandgap reference. Reference and channel choices take effect only once ADEN is set; with ADEN clear the ADC draws no power, so it should be turned off before power-saving sleep. The result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right adjusted unless ADLAR is set. For 8-bit work with ADLAR set, reading ADCH alone is enough. Otherwise read ADCL first: that locks both registers until ADCH is read, and a conversion finishing in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

With PRADC at zero, writing one to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC reads one until the conversion is done. A channel change made during a conversion waits until that conversion ends. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS (ADCSRB) resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, giving conversions at fixed intervals; an edge arriving during a conversion is ignored, and a trigger still high at the end starts nothing new. The trigger's interrupt flag is set whether or not its interrupt is enabled, and must be cleared before the next event can trigger.

Choosing the ADC interrupt flag as the trigger makes each conversion start the next as soon as it ends, whether or not ADIF is cleared. The first conversion is started by writing ADSC. With auto triggering on, ADSC can still start a single conversion, and it reads one during any conversion.

Full 10-bit resolution needs an ADC clock of 50 kHz to 200 kHz; a faster clock is allowed when fewer bits will do. A 7-bit prescaler, set by ADPS in ADCSRA, divides the CPU clock by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 and so suits any CPU clock above 100 kHz. It runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is low.

Writing ADSC starts a single conversion on the next ADC clock rising edge. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, with sample and hold at 1.5 clocks; the first one after ADEN is set takes 25 clocks to set up the analog circuits, sampling at 13.5 clocks. With the bandgap as input, give it time to settle or the first value read may be wrong. At the end the result is written, ADIF is set and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears. With auto triggering, the prescaler reset on the trigger gives a fixed delay: sampling comes 2 ADC clocks after the trigger's rising edge, and synchronisation adds 3 CPU clocks. In free running mode the next conversion begins at once while ADSC stays high.

MUXn and REFS1:0 pass through a buffer register, so a new choice takes hold only at a safe moment: it keeps updating until a conversion starts, freezes for the sampling time, and opens again in the last ADC clock before the conversion completes. Wait one ADC clock after writing ADSC before writing a new selection. When ADATE and ADEN are both set a trigger can arrive at any time, so ADMUX is safely changed only with ADATE or ADEN clear, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after its trigger, or after a conversion and before the trigger's interrupt flag is cleared; the new setting then applies to the next conversion.

In single conversion mode set the channel before starting; it may change one ADC clock after ADSC is written, though waiting for the end of the conversion is simplest. In free running mode set the channel before the first conversion; if it is changed after the first result, the conversion already under way still uses the old channel and the one after it the new.

VREF sets the conversion range; inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. It can be AVCC (through a passive switch), the internal 1.1 V (the bandgap VBG through an amplifier) or the AREF pin. AREF connects straight to the ADC in every case, so a capacitor from AREF to ground lowers noise, and VREF can be measured there with a high-impedance meter. VREF is a high-impedance node: only a capacitor may load it. With a fixed voltage on AREF the internal choices must not be used, as they would be shorted to it; with nothing on AREF the software may switch between AVCC and 1.1 V. Discard the first result after a reference change.

The ADC can convert while the CPU sleeps in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle mode, keeping CPU and I/O noise out. With the ADC enabled, idle, in single conversion mode and its interrupt enabled, entering one of those modes starts a conversion once the CPU halts. The ADC interrupt then wakes the CPU; if another interrupt wakes it first, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends, the CPU staying awake until the next sleep instruction. Other sleep modes do not stop the ADC, so clear ADEN before entering them.

Every ADCn pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected. When selected, the source charges a 14 pF sample and hold capacitor through a series resistance of 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ, biased at VCC/2. With a source of about 10 kΩ or less the sampling time is negligible; with a higher source impedance it depends on how long the source takes to charge the capacitor, which can vary widely. Low-impedance sources and slowly varying signals keep the charge moved into the capacitor small. Content above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) should be filtered out before the input.

Keep analog traces short, over the analog ground plane and away from fast digital lines. Feed AVCC from VCC through an LC network (10 µH series inductor, 100 nF to ground). Use the noise canceler. Any of ADC3...0 used as a digital output must not switch during a conversion; the 2-wire interface on ADC4 and ADC5 disturbs only conversions on those two channels.

An n-bit converter divides GND to VREF into 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n - 1. Offset is how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) lies from its ideal point at 0.5 LSB. Gain error, measured after removing offset, is how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) lies from its ideal point 1.5 LSB below full scale. Integral non-linearity is the largest deviation of any transition from ideal after offset and gain are removed. Differential non-linearity is the largest deviation of any code width from 1 LSB. The ideal value of each is 0 LSB. Quantization error is always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy is the largest deviation of any unadjusted transition from ideal, combining all the above; ideally ±0.5 LSB.

An on-chip temperature sensor sits on ADC channel 8, selected by MUX3...0 = 1000, and must be measured against the internal 1.1 V reference in single conversion mode. Its voltage rises about 1 mV per °C, and the reading is accurate to ±10 °C. The voltages vary from chip to chip; for better accuracy a calibration value measured per chip can be stored (in a register or EEPROM) and applied in software.

A one-wire, two-way debug link that controls program flow, executes AVR instructions in the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories. It offers full flow control, emulation of every on-chip function except the RESET pin, real-time and non-intrusive running, symbolic debugging in C, assembler or other languages, any number of software break points, and electrical behaviour identical to the plain part. It turns on when the DWEN fuse is programmed and the lock bits are unprogrammed: RESET becomes an open-drain two-way pin with its pull-up on, carrying the link to the emulator. The system clock stays whatever CKSEL selects.

Any pull-up on dW/RESET must be 10 kΩ or more, and none is needed. RESET tied straight to VCC stops the link. Capacitors on RESET and every external reset source must be disconnected while debugWIRE is in use.

Break points are BREAK instructions written into flash in place of the original instruction, which is kept and executed when the program resumes; a BREAK can also be placed in the program by hand. Each change of a break point reprograms the flash, which wears its data retention, so parts used for debugging should not be shipped.

dW shares its pin with RESET, so an external reset cannot be used while debugWIRE is on. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode and raises sleep current, so DWEN should be unprogrammed when debugWIRE is not in use. The DWDR register carries data from the running program to the debugger and is reachable only through debugWIRE.

These two parts have no read-while-write and no boot loader section: SPM runs from anywhere in flash, provided the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed. Code can fetch new firmware over any interface and write it itself. Flash is written a page at a time from a temporary page buffer, and a page must be erased before it is written. The buffer may be filled before a page erase (which allows read-modify-write: read the old page, change it, write it back) or between erase and write (the old data is then already gone). The buffer can be filled in any order; erase and write must address the same page. Part of a page is changed by saving the rest, for instance in the buffer, before the erase.

Each operation loads the Z pointer, writes a code to SPMCSR, then executes SPM within four clock cycles; disable interrupts first so the four-cycle window holds. Page erase: SPMCSR = 00000011, page address in PCPAGE of Z, R1:R0 ignored. Buffer fill: SPMCSR = 00000001, word in R1:R0, its place given by PCWORD of Z.
