Page write: SPMCSR = 00000101, page in PCPAGE, the other Z bits zero, R1:R0 ignored. The CPU halts during erase and write. Each buffer word can be written only once until the buffer is cleared, which happens after a page write, on writing RWWSRE, or on reset; an EEPROM write during buffer filling loses everything loaded.

The Z pointer (R31:R30) addresses SPM. The low bits of the program counter pick the word within a page and the high bits pick which page; erase and write are addressed separately, so software must give both the same page. LPM addresses flash byte by byte and so also uses Z0.
While the EEPROM is being written, flash programming by software and software reads of fuses and lock bits are blocked; check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuse and lock bits from software
operation.text: Load Z, set BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR, and execute LPM within three CPU cycles: Z = 0x0001 returns the lock bits, 0x0000 the fuse low byte, 0x0003 the fuse high byte and 0x0002 the extended fuse byte. BLBSET and SPMEN clear themselves when the read completes, or when no LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four. A programmed bit reads 0, an unprogrammed bit 1. On the ATmega48A/48PA only LB2 and LB1 exist in the lock byte; the boot loader parts return BLB12, BLB11, BLB02, BLB01, LB2, LB1 in bits 5 to 0, and their extended fuse byte in bits 3 to 0.

Too low a supply can corrupt flash in two ways: a write needs a minimum voltage to complete correctly, and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly. Any one of these avoids it: hold the part in reset while the supply is too low, using the brown-out detector if its level suits or an external supervisor otherwise (a write in progress finishes if the voltage holds up); keep the core in Power-down sleep while VCC is low, so nothing can write SPMCSR; and, on the boot loader parts, program the boot lock bits when the boot loader never needs updating.
Flash accesses from the CPU are timed by the calibrated RC oscillator.

A sample routine copies one page from RAM (Y pointer) to flash (Z pointer): it erases that page, fills the buffer word by word, writes that page and optionally reads it back to compare, calling one subroutine that waits for SPMEN to clear, disables interrupts, waits for any EEPROM write to end, then writes SPMCSR and executes SPM. RWWSB always reads zero on the ATmega48A/48PA; testing it anyway keeps code portable to the read-while-write parts.

On the ATmega88A/88PA/168A/168PA/328/328P a boot loader kept in flash can take in new code over any interface and write it, with true read-while-write. Code in the boot loader section can write all of flash, itself included, and so can even erase itself. The section size is set by fuses, and two independent sets of boot lock bits protect the application and boot loader sections. A page (its size is listed per device) is the unit of programming and has no effect on normal running.

Flash splits into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), sized by the BOOTSZ fuses and each with its own lock bits (boot lock bits 0 for the application, 1 for the BLS). SPM works only when executed from the BLS, so boot loader code must live there; from there it reaches all of flash.

Independently of BOOTSZ, flash is also split at a fixed address into an RWW section and an NRWW section. Erasing or writing a page in RWW lets the CPU keep running code from NRWW; erasing or writing a page in NRWW halts the CPU for the whole operation. The names refer to the section being programmed, not the one being read. Code in the RWW section can never be read during programming; a call, jump, LPM or interrupt into it may leave the software in an unknown state, so interrupts should be turned off or their vectors placed in the boot loader section, which always lies in NRWW. RWWSB in SPMCSR reads one while RWW is blocked, and software must clear it (by writing RWWSRE) before using RWW code again.

Without a boot loader the whole flash holds application code. The boot lock bits can protect all of flash, only the BLS, only the application section, or nothing, against updates by the MCU. Software, serial and parallel programming can set them; only a chip erase clears them. The general lock modes 1 and 2 do not govern LPM or SPM.

The application jumps or calls into the boot loader, for example on a command arriving by USART or SPI. Alternatively a programmed BOOTRST fuse points the reset vector at the boot loader start, so it runs after every reset. The MCU cannot change its own fuses: BOOTRST changes only through serial or parallel programming.

operation.topic: Z pointer use in the boot loader
operation.text: Once a programming operation starts its address is latched, freeing Z for other uses. Setting the boot loader lock bits is the only SPM operation that ignores Z.

operation.topic: SPM page operations, boot loader parts
operation.text: As on the ATmega48A/48PA, each operation loads Z, writes SPMCSR and executes SPM within four clock cycles. Page erase: SPMCSR = X0000011. Buffer fill: 00000001. Page write: X0000101. An erase or write aimed at the RWW section lets the NRWW section be read meanwhile; aimed at NRWW it halts the CPU. Buffer rules match: one write per word until cleared by page write, RWWSRE or reset, and an EEPROM write during filling loses the loaded data.
With the SPM interrupt enabled, it fires continuously while SPMEN is clear, replacing polling. The interrupt vectors should then sit in the BLS so no interrupt reaches the blocked RWW section.

Leaving boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed lets the boot loader be rewritten, and a stray write can then destroy it and block all future updates. Programming bit 11 protects it when it never needs changing.

operation.topic: Keeping off the RWW section during self-programming
operation.text: RWW is unreadable throughout a page erase or write, and software must not address it: move the vector table to the BLS or disable interrupts, and after programming clear RWWSB by writing RWWSRE before touching RWW.

Put the wanted bits in R0 (bit 7 and 6 = 1, then BLB12, BLB11, BLB02, BLB01, LB2, LB1), write X0001001 to SPMCSR, then SPM within four cycles; a zero programs that lock bit. Z is ignored, though 0x0001 is the value kept for compatibility, as is setting bits 7 and 6. All of flash stays readable while the lock bits are programmed.

operation.topic: Reading the signature row from software
operation.text: Load Z with the byte's address, set SIGRD and SPMEN in SPMCSR and execute LPM within three CPU cycles; the byte lands in the destination register. Both bits clear when the read completes or when no LPM follows within three cycles.

The read-while-write version of the sample page-copy routine erases, re-enables RWW, fills the buffer, writes that page, re-enables RWW, optionally verifies, and finally loops writing RWWSRE until RWWSB reads zero before returning to RWW code.

The ATmega48A/48PA has two lock bits (LB2, LB1); the other parts have six, adding BLB12, BLB11, BLB02 and BLB01. Each is unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), and only a chip erase returns them to 1. On the ATmega48A/48PA, with no separate boot section, SPM works across all of flash when the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed and not at all otherwise. Program fuses and boot lock bits before LB1 and LB2.
There are three fuse bytes: low, high and extended. A programmed fuse reads 0. Chip erase does not touch the fuses, and programming LB1 locks them, so set fuses before lock bits.

Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, so changes take effect only after leaving it; EESAVE is the exception and acts as soon as it is programmed. In normal mode the fuses are latched at power-up.

Every part has a three-byte signature, readable in serial and parallel mode even when locked, in an address space of its own. The high byte of address 0x000 in that space holds the internal RC oscillator calibration value, which is copied into OSCCAL during reset.

In parallel (high-voltage) programming the flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses are written and verified through named port pins (see the pin name mapping). Pulses last at least 250 ns unless stated otherwise. A positive pulse on XTAL1 does what XA1:XA0 select; a pulse on WR or OE executes the loaded command. VCC and AVCC take 4.5 V to 5.5 V, with AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC, and RESET takes 12 V.

Set the Prog_enable pins to 0000 and hold RESET and VCC at 0 V. Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V to VCC, which must pass 1.8 V within 20 µs. After 20 µs to 60 µs apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET. Hold Prog_enable for at least 10 µs more so it is latched, and wait at least 300 µs before the first command. If VCC cannot rise that fast: apply VCC, and as it passes 0.9 V to 1.1 V apply the 12 V to RESET, hold Prog_enable 10 µs, and wait for VCC to reach 4.5 V to 5.5 V before any command. Powering down or pulling RESET to 0 V leaves programming mode.

Command and address stay loaded, so a command is loaded once for many locations; 0xFF need not be written after a chip erase (to flash, and to EEPROM unless EESAVE kept it); and the address high byte needs reloading only when moving to a new 256-word flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, signature reads included.

Chip erase clears flash, EEPROM (kept if EESAVE is programmed) and lock bits, the lock bits only after flash is fully erased; fuses are unchanged. It must precede reprogramming flash or EEPROM. Sequence: XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 1000 0000, pulse XTAL1 high to load, pulse WR low to start (RDY/BSY goes low), and wait for RDY/BSY high before the next command.

A: load command 0001 0000 (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, pulse XTAL1). B: address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 0). C: data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01). D: load data high byte (BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01). E: with BS1 = 1, pulse PAGEL to latch the word. F: repeat B to E until the buffer is full. Low address bits pick the word within a page and high bits which page; when a page has fewer than 256 words the top bits of the low address byte form part of a page's address at page write. G: load address high byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 1). H: pulse WR low to program that page and wait for RDY/BSY high. I: repeat B to H for every page. J: load command 0000 0000 (no operation) to reset the internal write signals.

Load command 0001 0001, load address high then low byte, load the data byte and pulse PAGEL to latch it; repeat the address low, data and latch steps to fill the buffer. Then set BS1 = 0, pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY high before the next page.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of flash and EEPROM
operation.text: Flash: load command 0000 0010, address high and low bytes, set OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 to read the low byte on DATA, BS1 = 1 for the high byte, then OE = 1. EEPROM: command 0000 0011, address high and low, OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 to read the byte, then OE = 1.

Load command 0100 0000 and the new value as a data low byte (0 programs a bit, 1 erases it). For the low fuse byte pulse WR with BS1 = 0, BS2 = 0. For the high byte set BS1 = 1, BS2 = 0, pulse WR, then return BS1 to 0. For the extended byte set BS1 = 0, BS2 = 1, pulse WR, then return BS2 to 0. Each time wait for RDY/BSY high.

Load command 0010 0000 and a data low byte in which 0 programs a lock bit, pulse WR and wait for RDY/BSY high. Once LB1 and LB2 are both programmed (mode 3), no external mode can program the boot lock bits. Only chip erase clears lock bits.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration
operation.text: Load command 0000 0100 and set OE = 0; BS2:BS1 then select what DATA shows: 00 fuse low byte, 11 fuse high byte, 10 extended fuse byte, 01 lock bits (0 means programmed). Set OE = 1 to finish. Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, OE = 0 and BS1 = 0. Calibration byte: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00, OE = 0 and BS1 = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over SPI (SCK, MOSI in, MISO out) while RESET is held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction must come first. The programming pins are PB3, PB4 and PB5, which are not the internal SPI's pins on every part. VCC and AVCC take 1.8 V to 5.5 V, AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC. XTAL1 needs a clock only when the fuses select an external one. EEPROM writes erase each location automatically in serial mode, so no chip erase is needed first; chip erase sets every flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. SCK low and high times must each exceed 2 CPU clocks below 12 MHz and 3 CPU clocks at 12 MHz and above.

Data in is clocked on SCK's rising edge, data out on its falling edge. Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if SCK cannot be held low, pulse RESET high for at least two CPU clocks after SCK goes low. Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on MOSI. When in step, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third byte is sent; send all four bytes regardless, and if the echo is missing pulse RESET and try again. Flash is loaded a byte at a time into the buffer with the 6 LSB of the address (low byte before high byte for each word), then written with Write Program Memory Page carrying the 7 MSB of the address. EEPROM is written either a byte at a time with address and data, or a page at a time through Load EEPROM Memory Page and Write EEPROM Memory Page, which change only the bytes loaded. Without RDY/BSY polling, wait the tWD time before the next page or byte; touching the interface during a flash write can corrupt it. 0xFF need not be programmed into an erased part. Any location can be read back on MISO. End by setting RESET high to run, or RESET high then VCC off to power down.

Not every instruction applies to every part. Program memory instructions use word addresses, random within a page. A 1 in the LSB of the Poll RDY/BSY reply means an operation is still pending. Within a page, load the low data byte before the high byte. Unused fuses and lock bits should be left unprogrammed (1).
The highest clock frequency depends on VCC: 4 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.7 V and 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V, rising in a straight line from 1.8 V to 2.7 V and again from 2.7 V to 4.5 V.

operation.topic: Typical characteristics (-40 °C to 85 °C): how they are measured
operation.text: The typical-characteristics curves are not tested in production. Supply currents are taken with every I/O pin an input with its internal pull-up on, clocked from a rail-to-rail square-wave generator. For active and idle current every bit of PRR is set, so the modules it controls are off, and the analog comparator is off. Power-down current is the same whatever clock is selected. Supply voltage and clock frequency set the supply current most; pin loading, how often pins switch, the code running and ambient temperature also change it. Parts are characterised above their test-limit frequencies but are ensured to work only up to the frequency their ordering code gives. The watchdog timer draws the difference between power-down current with the watchdog on and with it off.

operation.topic: Supply current of the I/O modules
operation.text: Each module that PRR controls adds to the supply current in active and idle mode while its PRR bit is cleared. For the ATmega48A, ATmega48PA, ATmega88A and ATmega88PA the added current per module is given at VCC = 2 V and 1 MHz, 3 V and 4 MHz, and 5 V and 8 MHz, and also as a share of the active and of the idle current with an external clock; the shares serve for other supply voltages and frequencies. The total is the active or idle current times one plus the shares of the enabled modules.

operation.topic: Supply current of the I/O modules: ATmega168A, ATmega168PA, ATmega328, ATmega328P
operation.text: Each module that PRR controls adds to the supply current in active and idle mode while its PRR bit is cleared. For each of the ATmega168A, ATmega168PA, ATmega328 and ATmega328P one table gives the added current per module at VCC = 2 V and 1 MHz, 3 V and 4 MHz, and 5 V and 8 MHz; a second gives it as a percentage of the active and of the idle current with an external clock, for use at other supply voltages and frequencies. The ATmega168A and ATmega168PA share one set of figures, and the ATmega328 and ATmega328P another. The total is the active or idle current times one plus the percentages of the enabled modules.

operation.topic: Typical characteristics (-40 °C to 105 °C): how they are measured
operation.text: The ATmega48PA, ATmega88PA, ATmega168PA and ATmega328P have a second set of typical curves covering -40 °C to 105 °C. They are typical, not production tested. Supply currents are taken with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on. The ATmega48PA and ATmega88PA are clocked from a rail-to-rail square-wave generator, with every PRR bit set (its modules off) and the analog comparator off for active and idle current; the ATmega168PA and ATmega328P are clocked from a rail-to-rail sine-wave generator. Power-down current does not depend on the clock selected. Supply voltage and frequency set the current most; pin loading and switching, the code and temperature also change it. Parts are characterised above the frequencies they are tested to, but are only specified up to the frequency of their ordering code. The watchdog timer current is the power-down current with the watchdog on less the power-down current with it off.

The AVR core has arithmetic and logic, branch, bit and bit-test, data transfer and MCU control instructions, each with its operands, operation, affected SREG flags and cycle count. The hardware multiplies MUL, MULS and MULSU and the fractional forms FMUL, FMULS and FMULSU take 2 cycles. Conditional branches take 1 or 2 cycles and the compare-and-skip instructions 1, 2 or 3. Direct JMP (3 cycles) and CALL (4 cycles) are available only on the ATmega168PA and ATmega328P.

An ordering code is the device name, a dash, and a suffix for package and temperature range: AU 32A TQFP, MMH 28M1 VQFN, MU 32M1-A VQFN and PU 28P3 SPDIP for -40 °C to 85 °C; AN, MMN, MN and PN the same packages for -40 °C to 105 °C. A trailing R is tape and reel. Every code is listed at 20 MHz and a 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply, the frequency against supply voltage following the speed grades. The 105 °C range exists only for the PA and P devices; the ATmega168PA and ATmega328P have no 28M1 code at 105 °C. The ATmega328P-MU is the 32-pad 5 x 5 mm VQFN (32M1-A) for -40 °C to 85 °C.
